---
title: "Missing logbook stations — which vessels you cannot compute per-vessel figures for"
author: "Einar Hjörleifsson"
date: today
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(nanoparquet)
# quarto sets the working directory to this file's own; R/paths.R is the
# single place that resolves $FISHYDATA, and nothing here hardcodes a data path.
source("../R/paths.R")
loss <- read_parquet(fd_curated("check", "afli_rafr_stofn_loss.parquet"))
big  <- loss |> filter(stations_electronic >= 50)
```

## The short version

If you are computing anything **per vessel** from the logbook data for **2003–2019** —
effort, fishing footprint, CPUE, station counts, spatial distribution — then for
`r sum(!big$usable)` of the `r nrow(big)` vessels with enough electronic stations to judge, **the answer is
wrong, and the data does not tell you so.**

Some of their fishing stations are missing. Not flagged, not zero-filled, not marked
in any column: simply absent, as if those hauls never happened. For one vessel,
`r big$vessel[1]` (vid `r big$vid[1]`), **`r round(big$pct_lost[1])`% of its electronic
stations are gone**.

This page exists so you can check your vessel before you trust a number.

## Is my vessel affected?

```{r}
#| echo: false
big |>
  filter(!usable) |>
  transmute(vid, vessel, `call sign` = coalesce(cs, "—"), `LOA` = round(loa, 1),
            `stations recorded` = stations_electronic,
            `stations missing`  = stations_lost,
            `% missing`         = round(pct_lost, 1),
            `years`             = paste0(first_year, "–", last_year),
            severity) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Vessels absent from this table are at or near the 2.1% baseline, or have too few
electronic stations for a percentage to mean anything. The full table, including
those, is `curated/check/afli_rafr_stofn_loss.parquet`.

## What actually happened

Icelandic electronic logbook submissions arrive from the vessel into a feed table,
and the source system then merges that feed with the paper logbooks into a single
bookkeeping table. This repo reads the merged table, which is the right table to
read — reproducing the source faithfully is an adapter's job.

`r format(sum(loss$stations_lost), big.mark = ",")` submissions never made it across
that merge. They were never deleted; they carry positions, depths and catch records;
and their siblings from the very same submission did merge. Four explanations were
tested against the data and all four fail — they are not supersessions, not
resubmissions, not deletions, and not a transfer truncated partway.

**Why the loss is not being repaired.** Recovering the rows would mean this repo
asserting that the vessel feed is more complete than the source system's own
bookkeeping, on a guess at a mechanism that cannot be observed from here. A measured
gap is a more honest artefact than a repair built on a guess.

Recovering them was designed and then deliberately set aside: the evidence that they
are genuine hauls is strong, but nobody can say why the merge dropped them, and a
repair built on the wrong theory would be harder to find than the gap it filled. So
the data stays as it is and this page is the warning.

## The overall rate is not the story

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 8
loss |>
  filter(stations_electronic >= 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(pct_lost)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "grey30") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2.08, colour = "firebrick") +
  annotate("text", x = 3.2, y = Inf, label = "overall 2.08%", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6,
           colour = "firebrick", size = 3.2) +
  labs(x = "% of a vessel's electronic stations missing", y = "vessels",
       caption = "444 vessels with 50 or more electronic stations") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Overall, 2.08% of live electronic submissions are missing, which would be ignorable
if it were spread evenly. It is not. The median vessel loses about 1.3%, but the tail
is long: `r sum(big$pct_lost >= 5)` vessels lose 5% or more, `r sum(big$pct_lost >= 10)`
lose 10% or more, and `r sum(big$pct_lost >= 25)` lose a quarter or more.

In tonnage the loss is 0.09% of catch. **It is the event count that is wrong, not the
mass** — which is precisely why a catch-weighted sanity check will not detect it.

## It is a historical defect, and it healed

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 8
tibble(
  year = c(2003:2020),
  pct  = c(3.49, 19.14, 5.27, 5.14, 5.00, 6.28, 2.21, 2.81, 3.26, 2.35,
           2.20, 2.35, 1.53, 1.36, 1.52, 0.58, 0.02, 0.02)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, pct)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey30") + geom_point(colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2004, 2020, 4)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of that year's submissions missing") +
  theme_minimal()
```

As a *rate*, the loss is worst at the very beginning of electronic reporting — 19.1%
in 2004 — and declines steadily to 0.02% by 2019. The raw counts peak in 2008–2014
only because that is where the volume is. This looks like a reporting system maturing,
not an era with a distinct cause.

Two practical consequences. **Early years are the risky ones**: anything computed over
2004–2008 carries a 5–19% per-year loss, far above the headline. And **the recent data
is probably fine**: at 0.02% in 2019–2020, the defect had effectively stopped before
the feed table stopped being populated, so the 2020–2022 direct-load era most likely
does not carry it. That last point is an inference from the trend, not a measurement —
there is no feed to check those years against.

## Provenance

Built by `curate/checks/afli_rafr_stofn_loss.R` into
`curated/check/afli_rafr_stofn_loss.parquet`. The defect is declared in
`curate/corrections/afli_rafr_stofn_stations_dropped.yml`, which holds the full
characterisation and the decision not to repair it yet. The upstream report is tracked
as TODO item 19.
